raw_response:
I am 62 years old, I finished middle school, and I have farmed these 10.1 mu in Quzhou County alone for 40 years. My wife passed away years ago and my son works in Shijiazhuang, so it is just me. I cannot take risks anymore. Last year I planted 5 mu of cotton, 3 mu of chili, and 2.1 mu of mungbean, and I made enough to cover my costs and put some aside. That is exactly what I will do this year. At my age, changing crops is asking for trouble.

For cotton, I buy improved seeds from the dealer in town — the same kind Old Wang and most of my neighbors plant. It is not the cheapest bag, but I saw it handle the dry spell last summer better than the cheap stuff. For fertilizer, I put down one 50-kilogram bag of 15-15-15 compound fertilizer per mu as base fertilizer. Then I top-dress twice with urea: 15 kilograms per mu at flowering, and another 15 kilograms per mu at boll-setting. That works out to about 22 kilograms of nitrogen per mu, 7 kilograms of phosphorus, and 7 kilograms of potassium. I irrigate 4 times from my well: once when I sow in late April, once at flowering in July, once at peak boll-setting in early August, and once more in late August if the rain does not come. Cotton bollworm and aphids are terrible in this area, so I spray pesticides 7 times — I would rather spend the money than lose the whole crop to worms. I till the soil with a rotary tiller in mid-March to break up the winter crust. If the weather is normal, I expect about 340 kilograms of seed cotton per mu.

For chili, I plant 3 mu with hybrid seedlings that I buy from the dealer. I switched to hybrid two years ago after I saw Old Li's field — his fruit was bigger and the color was better at market. I transplant in late April. Chili needs potassium to fruit well, so I use one 50-kilogram bag of compound fertilizer per mu as base, then I add an extra 10 kilograms of potassium chloride per mu when the first flowers appear. I also top-dress twice with urea, about 10 kilograms per mu each time. Total that is about 20 kilograms of nitrogen per mu, 7 kilograms of phosphorus, and 12 kilograms of potassium. I irrigate 5 times because chili cannot stand drought when it is fruiting in July and August. I spray pesticides 5 times, mainly for spider mites and aphids that carry virus disease. I use the rotary tiller before transplanting. I expect about 2,600 kilograms of fresh chili per mu.

For mungbean on the remaining 2.1 mu, I plant in early June after the wheat would have come off — though I do not grow wheat, I plant mungbean directly. I save my own seeds from last year, so it is a traditional local variety. Mungbean makes its own nitrogen in the roots, so I learned at a village training years ago not to waste urea on it. I put down about 15 kilograms of compound fertilizer per mu at planting, which gives about 3 kilograms of nitrogen, 3 kilograms of phosphorus, and 3 kilograms of potassium per mu. I irrigate twice, once at flowering and once when the pods are filling. I spray twice for pod borers. Rotary tillage before sowing. I expect about 110 kilograms per mu.

I watch every yuan. Fertilizer prices have gone up again — a bag of urea cost me more last year than the year before — but I would rather put a little too much fertilizer than risk a bad harvest. If I lose yield, I lose thousands of yuan. If I waste 20 or 30 yuan of fertilizer, that is just a cost. I watch my neighbors closely. If Old Wang and the others are adding more, I add more. If they are cutting back, I get nervous. I hire three or four women from the village during cotton picking and chili harvest because I cannot do it all alone at 62. That costs me cash, so I cannot waste money on inputs I do not understand.
